subject: music
source_note: Topic structure follows the Edexcel A-Level Music specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships (exam boards do not publish these).

units.name: Performing
units.blurb: Building and presenting a recital through solo, ensemble and technology-based performance

units.name: Composing
units.blurb: Writing music to a set brief and developing compositional technique

units.name: Appraising
units.blurb: Listening, analysis and contextual study across the six areas of study

topics.name: Solo and/or Ensemble Performance
topics.blurb: Performing as a soloist or within an ensemble with accuracy, control and musicality

topics.name: Recital Programme (min. 8 minutes)
topics.blurb: Selecting and shaping a live recital of at least eight minutes

topics.name: Improvisation & Technology Realisation
topics.blurb: Improvising or realising music using music technology as a route to performance

topics.name: Composition to a Brief / Free Composition
topics.blurb: A composition responding to an area-of-study brief or a free composition (40 marks)

topics.name: Composition Assessing Technique
topics.blurb: A shorter composition to a brief testing handling of harmony, melody and texture (20 marks)

topics.name: Vocal Music
topics.blurb: Set works exploring word-setting, melody and texture in vocal writing

topics.name: Instrumental Music
topics.blurb: Set works built around idiomatic instrumental writing, form and structure

topics.name: Music for Film
topics.blurb: How music underscores, signals and shapes narrative on screen

topics.name: Popular Music and Jazz
topics.blurb: Style, harmony, rhythm and improvisation across popular and jazz set works

topics.name: Fusions
topics.blurb: Set works that blend traditions, drawing on world and Western influences

topics.name: New Directions
topics.blurb: Experimental and contemporary approaches that extend musical language

connections.why: Studying vocal set works deepens understanding of phrasing and word-setting that informs sung or melodic-line performance
Analysing idiomatic instrumental writing in the set works helps performers shape technique and interpretation
Jazz and popular set works model the harmonic and rhythmic language that underpins improvising over changes
Film scoring relies on technology and texture, the same toolkit used to realise music electronically
A brief linked to the Vocal Music area of study draws directly on its conventions of melody and accompaniment
Instrumental set works supply models of form and idiomatic writing for composing to a brief
Film-music techniques offer a clear stylistic brief for evoking mood and supporting narrative
Popular and jazz idioms are common briefs, giving harmonic and rhythmic frameworks to compose within
Both compositions share core craft, but the technical brief isolates and tests specific harmonic and contrapuntal skills
Vocal-style chorale and part-writing analysis builds the harmonic control assessed in the technical brief
Fusions draw heavily on popular and jazz idioms, blending them with other traditions
Both areas push beyond convention, combining or reinventing styles to extend the musical language
Experimental techniques from New Directions expand the textures and devices available when composing
The recital is assembled from solo and ensemble pieces shaped into a coherent eight-minute programme
Improvised or technology-realised pieces can form part of the assessed recital programme
Film scoring relies on orchestral and instrumental forces, so instrumental study illuminates the film repertoire
